metadata.title: STRUCTURED INTERVIEW SIGNALS AND WEIGHTS
metadata.subtitle: Observable Signal Checklist for Behavior Support Specialist / Early Childhood Teacher Interviews
metadata.generated_for: Behavior Support Specialist / Early Childhood Teacher
notes: Formatted in the same style as the attached weighted preschool teacher signals JSON.
Automatic no-hire signals are not numeric and override scoring.
Trait priority multipliers preserve the original rubric weighting: Critical x3, High x2, Medium x1.
Includes universal, infant/toddler, preschool, and Behavior Support Specialist track-specific traits.

The source rubric contains a possible inconsistency: preschool Trait 11 is named Patience and repeats the nonverbal-child question, while the canonical text mentions Structure & Flexibility. This file preserves the JSON trait as provided.
Revision 1.1 adds preschool-wide traits and subtle weak-answer patterns without collapsing the dictionary into a smaller master list.
revision_focus: Preserved existing trait/question-level organization and stable IDs where meanings remained the same.
Added subtle, realistic weak signals that candidates may reveal through vague, adult-centered, rigid, or compliance-focused answers.
Strengthened preschool-wide coverage for supervision, ratio awareness, family communication, adaptability, inclusion, and classroom group management.
Kept base_weight as the existing score field for compatibility with the uploaded structure.

critical_trait_rules: Immediate NO HIRE if any Critical trait raw score = 1
Any Critical raw score < 3 blocks Hire
scoring_logic.absolute_disqualifier_rule: Immediate NO HIRE if any automatic_no_hire signal is observed; continue interview but lock outcome.

behavior_support_specialist.label: Behavior Support Specialist / Early Childhood Teacher
gateway_requirements: Able to work full-time, in person
Comfortable serving both as behavior support and classroom teacher
Able to pass FBI, DOJ, and Child Abuse Index clearance
Experience supporting children with behavioral, developmental, social-emotional, sensory, or autism-related needs
ABA, RBT, BCBA-supervised, early intervention, special education, or similar experience preferred unless designated required by hiring team
Pediatric CPR / First Aid preferred or required before start, depending on school policy
recommended_question_set_30_minute: Tell me about a child whose behavior was challenging. How did you understand what was happening underneath the behavior?
Tell me about a time a child’s behavior was intense, such as screaming, aggression, elopement, or refusal. What did you do to manage yourself?
Walk me through what you would do if a child was dysregulated, pulling away, crying, or trying to run from the classroom.
How do you document behavior concerns without labeling or diagnosing the child?
A parent asks you, “Do you think my child has autism?” What would you say?
How would you support a teacher who says, “This child just does not listen and is ruining the class”?
This role includes working as a classroom teacher for ratio purposes. Tell me how you would shift between behavior support and regular classroom teaching.
Tell me about a time a supervisor or specialist gave you feedback about how you worked with a child. What did you do with that feedback?
behavior_support_specialist.source_note: Revision 1.1 calculates max_weighted_total from all traits applicable to the behavior_support_specialist track, including universal all-track traits and BSS-specific traits.

Comfortable serving both as behavior support and classroom teacher
Able to pass FBI, DOJ, and Child Abuse Index clearance

absolute_disqualifiers: Justifies yelling, shaming, intimidation, or force
Cynical or contemptuous language about children or families
Interviewing while supervising children or working
Burnout language with no ownership or recovery plan
Justifies yelling, shaming, intimidation, rough handling, or physical force
Describes children as manipulative, bad, spoiled, crazy, or intentionally malicious
Treats behavior support as controlling children rather than teaching skills
Claims they can diagnose autism, ADHD, trauma, or other conditions in this role
Minimizes supervision, licensing, safety, confidentiality, or documentation
Shows contempt for families, especially families who are hesitant about evaluation or services
Cannot describe how they regulate themselves during aggressive, loud, or stressful behavior
Says they do not need coaching, feedback, or supervision
Shows resentment toward children with special needs, sensory needs, speech delays, or behavior challenges
Cannot accept also working as a classroom teacher when not providing behavior support

traits.question: Tell me about a time a child was having a really hard moment emotionally. What did you notice about what they were feeling, and how did you respond?

core_signals.label: Frames behavior as communication
core_signals.evidence_hint: Candidate explicitly says the child was communicating a feeling, need, fear, overwhelm, or dysregulation.

core_signals.label: Names or infers the child’s feelings
core_signals.evidence_hint: Uses words such as overwhelmed, scared, frustrated, sad, tired, confused, or dysregulated.

core_signals.label: Uses warm, respectful language about the child
core_signals.evidence_hint: Speaks with dignity and avoids negative labels.

core_signals.label: Focuses on helping the child feel safe before compliance
core_signals.evidence_hint: Prioritizes emotional safety and co-regulation before rejoining the group.

core_signals.label: Acknowledges child autonomy or emotional experience
core_signals.evidence_hint: Validates the child’s experience instead of forcing emotional compliance.

core_signals.label: Dismisses or minimizes the child’s emotions
core_signals.evidence_hint: Says the child was fine, overreacting, dramatic, or should get over it.

core_signals.label: Labels child as bad, defiant, dramatic, manipulative, or attention-seeking
core_signals.evidence_hint: Uses problem-child or contemptuous language.

core_signals.label: Justifies yelling, shaming, intimidation, or force
core_signals.evidence_hint: Any defense of yelling, shaming, intimidation, rough handling, or force with children.

core_signals.label: Uses cynical or contemptuous language about children
core_signals.evidence_hint: Any demeaning language that shows contempt toward children.

extended_signals.label: Describes getting down to the child’s level
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions kneeling, sitting nearby, lowering body position, or joining calmly.

extended_signals.label: Uses calm voice, calm face, or calm body
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions soft tone, slow movement, calm face, or not escalating.

extended_signals.label: Balances support with helping child rejoin group
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Supports regulation first, then helps the child return to classroom expectations.

extended_signals.label: Appropriate answer but mostly behavior-management focused
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Safe steps are described, but emotional insight is limited.

extended_signals.label: Uses vague phrase like redirected without details
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Says redirected or calmed without describing words, actions, or reasoning.

extended_signals.label: Mentions rules before child emotion
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Lead emphasis is adult expectations rather than emotional understanding.

extended_signals.label: Focuses primarily on compliance or control
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Main goal is making the child comply rather than understand or support.

extended_signals.label: Gives safe-sounding empathy language without an example
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Says they comfort, support, or validate children but cannot describe what they noticed or did.

extended_signals.label: Redirects without naming the child’s need or feeling
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Moves quickly to redirecting behavior without showing emotional attunement.

extended_signals.label: Frames distress as attention-seeking without curiosity
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Suggests the child wanted attention but does not explore fear, need, overwhelm, fatigue, or communication.

suggested_follow_up_probes: What do you think the child was feeling in that moment?
What did you do to help the child feel safe?
What did you say to the child?

traits.question: Tell me about a time you felt overwhelmed or stressed at work with children present. What did you do to manage, not the kids, but yourself and your stress?

core_signals.label: Acknowledges stress without blaming children
core_signals.evidence_hint: Owns the adult emotional state as theirs to manage.

core_signals.label: Names specific self-regulation strategy
core_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions breathing, pausing, grounding, lowering voice, slowing down, or asking for help.

core_signals.label: Recognizes adult regulation affects children
core_signals.evidence_hint: Connects adult tone, body, and regulation to children’s regulation and safety.

core_signals.label: Takes ownership of tone, body language, and reactions
core_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions keeping voice steady, body calm, and response controlled.

core_signals.label: Says anyone would lose it
core_signals.evidence_hint: Normalizes loss of control around children.

core_signals.label: Admits snapping without ownership or repair
core_signals.evidence_hint: No accountability, repair, or prevention described.

core_signals.label: Normalizes yelling or harsh tone
core_signals.evidence_hint: Suggests yelling, harshness, or snapping is normal in childcare.

core_signals.label: Admits yelling, shaming, intimidation, or losing control without accountability
core_signals.evidence_hint: Unsafe adult emotional behavior with no ownership or correction.

core_signals.label: Cannot identify any way to regulate self around children
core_signals.evidence_hint: No safe self-regulation method after probing.

core_signals.label: Burnout language with no ownership or recovery plan
core_signals.evidence_hint: Expresses burnout, resentment, or inability to cope with no responsible plan.

extended_signals.label: Describes internal warning signs
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Names rising stress, tension, irritation, racing thoughts, or voice change.

extended_signals.label: Asks for support appropriately while preserving supervision
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Gets help without leaving children unsupported.

extended_signals.label: Says stayed calm but cannot explain how
extended_signals.evidence_hint: No strategy, cue, or follow-through described.

extended_signals.label: Says they just got through it
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Endures stress but does not describe regulation.

extended_signals.label: Focuses on managing children instead of managing self
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Answer misses the self-regulation focus.

extended_signals.label: Blames children for adult stress reaction
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Explains adult dysregulation as caused by children or chaos.

extended_signals.label: Professes patience but gives no real stress example
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Uses general statements like I am patient without describing an actual stressful moment.

extended_signals.label: Relies on personality trait instead of regulation strategy
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Says they are naturally calm or patient but gives no concrete self-regulation method.

extended_signals.label: Describes stress spilling into tone with limited repair
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Acknowledges irritation, sharp tone, or visible frustration but gives weak repair or prevention.

suggested_follow_up_probes: What was going on internally for you?
How did you keep your voice and body calm?
What would children have seen from you?

traits.question: Imagine you’re caring for a child who clearly does not want to be touched during a routine task, like diapering, helping with clothing, or guiding them physically. They are pulling away or crying. Walk me through exactly what you would do and say, step by step

core_signals.label: Recognizes pulling away or crying as communication
core_signals.evidence_hint: Treats resistance as communication rather than defiance.

core_signals.label: Uses consent-oriented language
core_signals.evidence_hint: Uses phrases like I see you do not want this, I will go slowly, or offers choices.

core_signals.label: Uses respectful language about body and dignity
core_signals.evidence_hint: Shows respect for the child’s body, privacy, and discomfort.

core_signals.label: Balances hygiene, licensing, safety, and emotional respect
core_signals.evidence_hint: Completes necessary care without ignoring distress.

core_signals.label: Maintains safety without threats or force
core_signals.evidence_hint: Keeps the child safe without intimidation or overpowering.

core_signals.label: Minimizes the child’s discomfort
core_signals.evidence_hint: Treats distress as unimportant, excessive, or manipulative.

core_signals.label: Describes forcing, overpowering, dragging, or restraining the child
core_signals.evidence_hint: Non-emergency force or restraint to complete routine care or gain compliance.

core_signals.label: Disregards licensing, supervision, or safety standards
core_signals.evidence_hint: States or implies required safety standards can be ignored.

extended_signals.label: Slows down instead of rushing
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Pauses, waits, or reduces pressure.

extended_signals.label: Narrates actions before touching or moving child
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Explains what will happen before acting.

extended_signals.label: Offers simple choices when possible
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Offers safe choices about sequence, helper, item, or timing.

extended_signals.label: Rule-compliant answer without emotional insight
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Follows steps but does not acknowledge child experience.

extended_signals.label: Uses they have to or not a choice as main message
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Centers control instead of safety plus dignity.

extended_signals.label: Focuses on adult convenience over child dignity
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Emphasizes speed, schedule, or adult ease over the child’s experience.

extended_signals.label: Complains that safety or child-rights rules are excessive
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Shows resentment toward standards.

extended_signals.label: Says child must learn routines without explaining support
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Emphasizes routine compliance without describing choices, narration, pacing, or dignity.

extended_signals.label: Offers comfort after task but not during task
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Completes care first and only addresses distress afterward.

extended_signals.label: Cannot explain step-by-step safety and dignity
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Cannot describe what they would say or do during sensitive physical care after probing.

suggested_follow_up_probes: What exact words would you use?
How would you keep the child safe without forcing them?
When would you ask for help?

traits.question: Tell me about a time you received constructive criticism or feedback you didn’t expect or didn’t fully agree with. What happened next?

core_signals.label: Describes specific change made after feedback
core_signals.evidence_hint: Names what they changed in practice.

core_signals.label: Takes responsibility for improvement
core_signals.evidence_hint: Owns growth instead of focusing on unfairness.

core_signals.label: Shows reflective growth from feedback
core_signals.evidence_hint: Explains what they learned and how it affected their work.

core_signals.label: Says feedback was wrong or unfair without reflection
core_signals.evidence_hint: Rejects feedback without considering any valid point.

core_signals.label: Blames supervisor, coworker, or parent
core_signals.evidence_hint: Explains situation primarily through others being wrong.

core_signals.label: Cannot name any constructive feedback received
core_signals.evidence_hint: No real example after probing.

core_signals.label: Rejects supervision or feedback outright
core_signals.evidence_hint: States they do not need or will not accept supervision.

core_signals.label: States they do not need coaching
core_signals.evidence_hint: Clear resistance to coaching or supervision.

extended_signals.label: Acknowledges feedback felt uncomfortable
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Can name discomfort without becoming defensive.

extended_signals.label: Listens before defending
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Describes pausing, asking questions, or trying to understand.

extended_signals.label: Mentions following up with supervisor or mentor
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Returns for clarification or checks progress.

extended_signals.label: Says they accepted feedback but gives no change example
extended_signals.evidence_hint: No observable adjustment described.

extended_signals.label: Describes compliance rather than growth
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Followed feedback only because required.

extended_signals.label: Shows resentment toward supervision
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Tone or language suggests coaching is unwelcome.

extended_signals.label: Gives polished feedback answer without a specific event
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Sounds open to feedback but provides no concrete situation or changed behavior.

extended_signals.label: Accepts feedback only from certain authorities
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Implies feedback matters only if it comes from a director, specialist, or person they respect.

extended_signals.label: Interprets feedback as personal criticism
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Talks mainly about feeling attacked, judged, or disrespected rather than learning.

suggested_follow_up_probes: What did you change after receiving the feedback?
Did you agree with it at first?
What did you learn?

traits.question: Tell me about a time something, such as a lesson plan, did not go as expected and your role in it.

core_signals.label: Clearly owns their role in what happened
core_signals.evidence_hint: Identifies their own contribution without over-blaming others.

core_signals.label: Describes corrective action
core_signals.evidence_hint: Names what they did to fix or stabilize the situation.

core_signals.label: Reflects on how to prevent recurrence
core_signals.evidence_hint: Explains what they changed for next time.

core_signals.label: Says that was not on me
core_signals.evidence_hint: Denies personal responsibility.

core_signals.label: Blames children, coworkers, parents, or schedule
core_signals.evidence_hint: Primary explanation is outside blame.

core_signals.label: Denies they could have done anything differently
core_signals.evidence_hint: No insight into personal role after probing.

core_signals.label: Describes disregard for safety, supervision, or licensing expectations
core_signals.evidence_hint: Reliability failure involved safety or licensing disregard.

core_signals.label: Describes leaving children unsupported or unsupervised
core_signals.evidence_hint: Any supervision failure without appropriate response.

extended_signals.label: Communicates quickly when something goes wrong
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Tells director, coworker, or family promptly when appropriate.

extended_signals.label: Follows through after the issue
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Completes fix, documentation, or plan.

extended_signals.label: Balances context with accountability
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Explains circumstances while still owning their part.

extended_signals.label: Partial ownership mixed with external factors
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Some ownership but diluted by context.

extended_signals.label: Takes responsibility in words but gives no prevention plan
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Cannot name a next step.

extended_signals.label: Minimizes their responsibility
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Downplays their role while emphasizing circumstances.

extended_signals.label: Gives general reliability claim with no example
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Says they are reliable, punctual, or accountable but does not give evidence.

extended_signals.label: Fixes immediate problem but gives no documentation or follow-up
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Stabilizes the moment but does not explain communication, documentation, or prevention.

extended_signals.label: Minimizes pattern as one-time thing without reflection
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Dismisses the issue as not a big deal or unlikely to happen again without a prevention plan.

suggested_follow_up_probes: What was your role?
What did you do to fix it?
What did you change afterward?

traits.question: Tell me about a time you had a challenge with another adult. How did you navigate it?

core_signals.label: Keeps children’s needs central
core_signals.evidence_hint: Frames adult conflict around what is best for children.

core_signals.label: Describes direct professional communication
core_signals.evidence_hint: Talked directly, calmly, and appropriately with the adult.

core_signals.label: Reflects on own contribution to conflict
core_signals.evidence_hint: Names what they did or could have done differently.

core_signals.label: Says they prefer working alone
core_signals.evidence_hint: Preference appears incompatible with classroom teamwork.

core_signals.label: Speaks contemptuously about coworkers
core_signals.evidence_hint: Uses demeaning, sarcastic, or hostile language about adults.

core_signals.label: Describes repeated conflicts without ownership
core_signals.evidence_hint: Conflict appears recurrent and externally blamed.

core_signals.label: Describes hostile adult interactions around children
core_signals.evidence_hint: Adult conflict compromised children’s emotional safety.

core_signals.label: Indicates they cannot work safely or professionally with a team
core_signals.evidence_hint: States or demonstrates inability to function in team-based childcare setting.

extended_signals.label: Speaks respectfully about the other adult
extended_signals.evidence_hint: No contempt or demeaning language.

extended_signals.label: Focuses on shared responsibility
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Uses collaborative framing and avoids blame.

extended_signals.label: Listens to other person’s perspective
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions hearing the other person out.

extended_signals.label: Involves supervisor appropriately when needed
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Escalates appropriately rather than gossiping or triangulating.

extended_signals.label: Focuses on coexistence rather than teamwork
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Got through it but did not collaborate meaningfully.

extended_signals.label: Describes doing their own job and letting others do theirs
extended_signals.evidence_hint: May indicate low collaboration.

extended_signals.label: Blames the other adult entirely
extended_signals.evidence_hint: No ownership or curiosity about the other adult’s view.

extended_signals.label: Describes avoiding conflict rather than resolving it
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Keeps peace but does not communicate, clarify expectations, or repair teamwork.

extended_signals.label: Uses director as default for routine adult issues
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Escalates ordinary coworker tension without first attempting respectful direct communication.

extended_signals.label: Gossips or triangulates instead of addressing issue
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Talks to others about the problem rather than using professional channels.

suggested_follow_up_probes: What did you say to the other adult?
What part was yours to own?
How did you keep the focus on children?

traits.question: Can you share something you’ve learned about children or yourself over time that changed how you approach your work?

core_signals.label: Explains how their approach changed

core_signals.label: Describes specific insight about children or self
core_signals.evidence_hint: Provides an insight, not just a generic statement.

core_signals.label: Says they already know what works
core_signals.evidence_hint: Signals fixed mindset and low openness to learning.

core_signals.label: Shows rigid beliefs about how children should behave
core_signals.evidence_hint: Emphasizes children should act a certain way without developmental reflection.

core_signals.label: Rejects learning, coaching, or child-centered practice
core_signals.evidence_hint: States they do not need to learn, adjust, or be coached.

core_signals.label: Expresses fixed punitive or contemptuous beliefs about children
core_signals.evidence_hint: Rigid or punitive views undermine child-centered care.

extended_signals.label: Shows growth mindset
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Open to learning, adjusting, and improving.

extended_signals.label: Reflects on emotional presence, not just activities
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Recognizes adult emotional presence matters.

extended_signals.label: Connects learning to better child support
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Explains how learning helped children.

extended_signals.label: Acknowledges experience changed assumptions
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Identifies something they used to think differently.

extended_signals.label: Says always learning but gives no example
extended_signals.evidence_hint: General growth language without evidence.

extended_signals.label: Describes learning by doing without insight
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Experience is described but no meaningful learning is named.

extended_signals.label: Focuses on classroom tricks only
extended_signals.evidence_hint: No deeper developmental or emotional reflection.

extended_signals.label: Says approach has not changed
extended_signals.evidence_hint: No meaningful professional growth described.

extended_signals.label: Names training or experience but no practice change
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions classes, years of experience, or credentials without explaining how practice changed.

extended_signals.label: Dismisses new methods as theory
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Contrasts real-world experience against developmentally appropriate or child-centered practices.

suggested_follow_up_probes: What changed in your actual practice?

traits.question: Tell me about how you physically care for infants or toddlers during routines like feeding, diapering, or comforting.

core_signals.evidence_hint: Slows down or changes approach when child resists or is distressed.

core_signals.label: Says you have to be quick as main strategy
core_signals.evidence_hint: Prioritizes speed over cues, dignity, or gentleness.

core_signals.label: Treats crying as background noise

core_signals.label: Describes using force to complete routines

extended_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions slow movement or calm pace.

extended_signals.evidence_hint: Procedural answer with limited attunement.

extended_signals.label: Describes completing routines efficiently but not harshly

traits.question: How do you understand what a nonverbal child needs when they’re crying or upset? Can you walk me through how you respond in those moments?

core_signals.evidence_hint: Does not treat nonverbal communication as lesser or annoying.

traits.question: Tell me about a time a child’s behavior was challenging for you. How did you approach it?

core_signals.evidence_hint: Misunderstands behavior support.

core_signals.label: Ignores safety-critical behavior plan follow-through
core_signals.evidence_hint: Could create safety risk if plan involves elopement, aggression, or supervision.

extended_signals.label: Adjusts based on results
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Plan is reviewed and improved.

extended_signals.label: Understands consistency but gives limited detail
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Concept is present but implementation unclear.

extended_signals.label: Relies on reminders rather than systems
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Weak follow-through structure.

extended_signals.label: Blames staff without coaching or support
extended_signals.evidence_hint: No collaborative implementation.

extended_signals.label: Plan depends on one adult instead of team system
extended_signals.evidence_hint: The plan works only if one person remembers it, with no classroom-wide handoff or follow-up.

suggested_follow_up_probes: How did you communicate the plan to others?
How did you check whether it was working?
What did you do if staff were inconsistent?

traits.trait_name: Supervision, Ratio Awareness & Active Safety Scanning
traits.question: Tell me about how you keep a classroom safe when several children need attention at the same time. What are you watching, and how do you decide what to do first?

core_signals.label: Names active supervision strategies
core_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions scanning, positioning, counting children, anticipating risk areas, and moving intentionally.

core_signals.label: Maintains ratio and group awareness while helping one child
core_signals.evidence_hint: Explains how they support an individual child without losing awareness of the rest of the group.

core_signals.label: Prioritizes immediate safety with calm follow-through
core_signals.evidence_hint: Identifies safety risks first while staying calm and organized.

core_signals.label: Anticipates common risks before incidents happen
core_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions doors, climbing, choking hazards, bathrooms, playground zones, conflict areas, or transitions.

core_signals.label: Talks about safety generally without concrete actions
core_signals.evidence_hint: Says they watch the children or keep them safe but gives no specific supervision behaviors.

core_signals.label: Focuses on one child and loses group awareness
core_signals.evidence_hint: Answer suggests tunnel vision that could leave other children unsupervised.

core_signals.label: Cannot explain how to maintain ratio or get help
core_signals.evidence_hint: Does not know how to preserve supervision coverage when a child needs intensive support.

core_signals.label: Disregards ratio, supervision, or licensing requirements
core_signals.evidence_hint: States or implies ratios, supervision, or licensing standards can be ignored when inconvenient.

extended_signals.label: Uses positioning to see doors, corners, and high-risk areas
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Describes where they stand or move so they can see children and risk areas.

extended_signals.label: Counts children during transitions
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions head counts, name-to-face checks, or transition counts.

extended_signals.label: Communicates with coworkers before moving away
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Checks coverage before stepping away, helping a child, or changing zones.

extended_signals.label: Over-relies on director for routine supervision decisions
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Calls leadership before using ordinary classroom safety judgment.

extended_signals.label: Cannot explain documentation after safety incident
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Does not mention reporting, documentation, parent communication, or director notification when needed.

suggested_follow_up_probes: Where would you position yourself?
What would you do if one child bolts while another child is crying?
How do you make sure ratio is maintained?

traits.question: Tell me about a time you had to manage a group of young children during a transition, busy classroom moment, or activity that was starting to fall apart. What did you do?

core_signals.label: Uses preventive structure and clear routines
core_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions routines, visual cues, preparation, songs, jobs, or predictable steps.

core_signals.label: Adjusts activity to children’s attention and development
core_signals.evidence_hint: Changes length, pace, materials, or expectations based on age and group state.

core_signals.label: Balances warmth with clear limits
core_signals.evidence_hint: Shows both connection and boundaries.

core_signals.label: Uses redirection and engagement before consequences
core_signals.evidence_hint: Re-engages children through modeling, choices, movement, or meaningful tasks.

core_signals.label: Gives safe-sounding but vague group-management answer
core_signals.evidence_hint: Says they redirect, keep control, or use routines but cannot describe observable steps.

core_signals.label: Focuses on obedience or control over engagement
core_signals.evidence_hint: Main goal is quiet, compliance, or control rather than teaching group skills.

core_signals.label: Expects long sitting or listening beyond developmental level
core_signals.evidence_hint: Uses expectations that are unrealistic for preschoolers or toddlers.

core_signals.label: Uses shaming, threats, or public humiliation to control group
core_signals.evidence_hint: Relies on fear, embarrassment, or intimidation as classroom management.

extended_signals.label: Uses transition warnings or visuals
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions timers, pictures, songs, first-then language, or previewing transitions.

extended_signals.label: Gives children roles or choices during group moments
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Uses helpers, jobs, limited choices, or participation to increase engagement.

extended_signals.label: Resets group with movement or sensory input
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Uses movement, outdoor time, sensory support, or calm reset when the group is dysregulated.

extended_signals.label: Relies on repeating directions louder
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Repeats or raises voice instead of changing strategy.

extended_signals.label: Sends children out as primary group-management tool
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Uses removal or exclusion instead of adapting the environment and teaching skills.

suggested_follow_up_probes: What did you do before the transition started?
How did you adjust when the group was losing focus?
What would children hear you say?

traits.question: Tell me about a time you had to communicate with a parent or guardian about a child’s day, behavior, injury, concern, or progress. How did you handle it?

core_signals.label: Communicates factually, respectfully, and promptly
core_signals.evidence_hint: Uses objective language, timely communication, and a respectful tone.

core_signals.label: Balances concerns with child strengths and supports
core_signals.evidence_hint: Does not reduce the child to a problem; includes what adults are doing to help.

core_signals.label: Knows when to involve director or follow center policy
core_signals.evidence_hint: Recognizes boundaries for injuries, incidents, sensitive concerns, or formal documentation.

core_signals.label: Listens to parent perspective without defensiveness
core_signals.evidence_hint: Invites parent input and stays calm if the parent is upset.

core_signals.label: Gives generic parent communication answer with no example
core_signals.evidence_hint: Says they are professional or communicate well but gives no concrete example.

core_signals.label: Blames parents for child behavior
core_signals.evidence_hint: Attributes the concern mainly to parenting, home life, or lack of discipline.

core_signals.label: Shares judgmental or confidential information inappropriately
core_signals.evidence_hint: Answer suggests gossip, unnecessary detail, or confidentiality concerns.

core_signals.label: Shows contempt or hostility toward families
core_signals.evidence_hint: Uses demeaning language about parents or families, especially around disability, culture, discipline, or socioeconomic status.

extended_signals.label: Uses objective examples instead of labels
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Describes what happened rather than calling the child aggressive, bad, lazy, spoiled, or difficult.

extended_signals.label: Offers next steps or partnership
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Explains what the classroom will try and how the family can share helpful context.

extended_signals.label: Adapts communication for language access
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions translation, bilingual staff, written notes, or checking understanding.

extended_signals.label: Overpromises or operates outside role
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Promises outcomes, gives diagnosis, or handles sensitive matters without appropriate supervisor involvement.

extended_signals.label: Avoids parent communication due to discomfort
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Relies on others for routine communication they should be able to handle.

suggested_follow_up_probes: What exact words would you use with the parent?
When would you involve the director?
How would you avoid labeling the child?

traits.question: Preschool work changes quickly. Tell me about a time your plan changed, staffing shifted, or the classroom needed something different than expected. How did you respond?

core_signals.label: Adjusts plan without losing calm or quality
core_signals.evidence_hint: Changes approach while maintaining safety, warmth, and professionalism.

core_signals.label: Stays child-centered during changes
core_signals.evidence_hint: Keeps children’s needs central when schedule, staffing, or activities change.

core_signals.label: Follows through on tasks, communication, and handoffs
core_signals.evidence_hint: Completes responsibilities and communicates changes clearly.

core_signals.label: Shows readiness for physical and practical classroom demands
core_signals.evidence_hint: Understands standing, sitting on floor, lifting within policy, cleaning, routines, and active engagement.

core_signals.label: Says flexible but gives no real example
core_signals.evidence_hint: Claims adaptability without a concrete situation or actions.

core_signals.label: Becomes rigid when plans change
core_signals.evidence_hint: Shows frustration, resistance, or inability to adjust when children or classroom needs shift.

core_signals.label: Views routine care or classroom tasks as not their job
core_signals.evidence_hint: Rejects ordinary preschool duties such as cleaning, transitions, toileting support within role, or classroom coverage.

core_signals.label: Cannot accept core role requirements
core_signals.evidence_hint: States they cannot perform essential supervision, caregiving, teamwork, schedule, or in-person classroom requirements.

extended_signals.label: Communicates changes to team clearly
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Updates coworkers or supervisor about changes, needs, and handoffs.

extended_signals.label: Reprioritizes based on safety and child needs
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Can decide what matters first in a changing classroom.

extended_signals.label: Asks for help without abdicating responsibility
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Gets support while still owning their role.

extended_signals.label: Over-relies on scripted plans
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Struggles when the day requires deviation from prepared activities or exact routines.

extended_signals.label: Shows low-energy or passive role concept
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Describes preschool work as mainly watching children rather than active engagement and supervision.

suggested_follow_up_probes: What changed from your original plan?
How did you decide what mattered first?
What did you communicate to the team?

traits.question: Tell me about a time you worked with a child who needed something different from the rest of the group, such as language support, sensory support, extra help with transitions, or developmental support. What did you do?

core_signals.label: Adapts support to child need without isolating child
core_signals.evidence_hint: Makes accommodations while keeping the child included in classroom life.

core_signals.label: Uses strength-based respectful language
core_signals.evidence_hint: Speaks about children with different needs respectfully and without pity or blame.

core_signals.label: Uses visuals, sensory supports, choices, or modified expectations
core_signals.evidence_hint: Names practical supports for developmental, communication, sensory, or behavioral needs.

core_signals.label: Collaborates with family, team, or specialists within role
core_signals.evidence_hint: Recognizes teamwork and role boundaries when supporting a child with different needs.

core_signals.label: Gives kind but generic inclusion answer
core_signals.evidence_hint: Says every child is different or they treat everyone equally but gives no actual support strategy.

core_signals.label: Treats different needs as misbehavior or bad parenting
core_signals.evidence_hint: Attributes sensory, language, developmental, or behavioral needs to defiance, spoiling, or parenting failure.

core_signals.label: Expects child to fit program without adaptation
core_signals.evidence_hint: Places responsibility mainly on child to keep up, listen, or adapt.

core_signals.label: Shows resentment toward children with different needs
core_signals.evidence_hint: Uses contemptuous or exclusionary language about children with disability, sensory, language, behavioral, or developmental needs.

extended_signals.label: Notices sensory or communication triggers
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Mentions sound, transitions, crowds, hunger, fatigue, language, or communication demands.

extended_signals.label: Embeds support in normal classroom routines
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Uses inclusive supports during play, transitions, meals, toileting, or group time.

extended_signals.label: Uses equality language when equity is needed
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Says all children should be treated the same without recognizing individualized supports.

extended_signals.label: Removes child from group too quickly
extended_signals.evidence_hint: Uses separation as a default rather than adapting expectations or supports.

suggested_follow_up_probes: What did you change for that child?
How did you keep the child included?
How did you communicate with the team or family?

global_red_flags.label: Justifies yelling, shaming, intimidation, rough handling, restraint, dragging, grabbing, or force
Minimizes children’s rights, dignity, safety, supervision, licensing, confidentiality, or documentation
Claims they can diagnose autism, ADHD, trauma, sensory processing disorder, or other conditions
Says they do not need coaching, feedback, or supervision
Cannot describe how they regulate themselves during aggression, screaming, elopement, or refusal
Uses contemptuous language about children with behavioral, developmental, sensory, speech, or special needs
Shows contempt for families, especially families hesitant about evaluation or services
Refuses classroom teacher duties when not providing behavior support
Uses bad, spoiled, manipulative, crazy, defiant, dramatic, or attention-seeking language
Focuses on control before safety, regulation, relationship, or teaching
Gives vague answers and cannot add detail after probing
Skips the child’s emotional experience or adult’s internal self-regulation

global_strong_candidate_signals.label: Looks for unmet needs, lagging skills, sensory needs, communication barriers, and environmental triggers
Speaks about children warmly and respectfully
Prioritizes safety, dignity, and emotional security
Regulates own voice, body, face, and pace during stress
Teaches replacement skills instead of relying on punishment
Uses visuals, routines, first-then supports, modeling, sensory supports, and co-regulation
Documents objectively without labels or diagnosis
Communicates with parents using strengths, observations, compassion, and follow-up
Supports teachers through modeling, practical strategies, and follow-up without shaming
Understands the dual role of behavior support and classroom teaching while protecting ratio

dictionary_design_rules: Signals describe observable content in candidate answers, not personality diagnoses.
Positive and negative signals should be inferable from what the candidate says, implies, or fails to explain after reasonable probing.
Negative signals should capture realistic weak-answer patterns, including vague safe language, adult-centered framing, compliance focus, lack of examples, weak prevention, and poor follow-through.
Automatic no-hire signals are reserved for unsafe, contemptuous, legally risky, or role-incompatible statements.
Critical flags mark serious concerns that require careful review, targeted follow-up, or possible disqualification.
Weights reflect preschool job relevance: child safety, emotional attunement, self-regulation, and rights-sensitive care carry the highest concern.
